title: POC dedicated capacity sizing + autoscale cost workshop notes
content:
Context / objective:
We ran a 90-minute internal workshop to align on a customer-facing POC for dedicated capacity: sizing guidance, autoscaling policy templates, and a set of baseline GPU cost estimates to include in proposals. This doc captures the working notes, quick calculations we used during the call, and action items for follow-up artifacts (proposal template + CR).

Customer profile (target POC):
- Mid-market SaaS (fintech vertical) planning to add contextual chat, document search + summarization to their product.
- Traffic shape (customer provided): 3k peak concurrent end-users, average session generates ~250 tokens outgoing (model prompts) and ~800 tokens generated per session. Session concurrency converts roughly to 9k active simultaneous model requests at busy times (they route chat messages in near-real-time).
- Latency SLO: p95 < 900ms for short-turn responses (<= 200 tokens), p95 < 2.5s for long responses (>= 400 tokens).
- Security: Requires Private or Dedicated (no public multi-tenant). Will look at Dedicated initially.

Assumptions we used in the workshop (call these out explicitly):
- Model family: customer prefers an open/Redwood-verified model. We sized two variants: "large-medium" (13B / 16-28GB) and "large" (70B / 80+GB). We documented a fallback ladder (13B for cold fallback, 70B for quality-critical routes).
- Tokenization: assume average 3.5 characters/token, roughly 4 tokens per word.
- GPU choices: H100 80GB equivalent (best throughput for 70B), A100 40GB equivalent (good price/perf for 13B), and an 80GB A100-like option for larger 30-40B midpoints.
- Throughput baseline from lab runs (customer workload style):
  - 13B quantized (fp16 + q4/8): ~250–400 tokens/sec per A100-40GB equiv (batching enabled; 1–4 request batches typical for latency SLO).
  - 70B (h100 80GB equiv): ~700–1200 tokens/sec per GPU (highly variable with kv caching; these are optimistic upper-range bursts).
- Average generation length to budget: 800 tokens (customer average); treat p95 200 tokens as common short-turn case.
- Effective utilization target: we design to 65% steady-state GPU utilization to allow headroom for bursts and background housekeeping.

Sizing worked example (short-turn p95 case, 200 tokens target):
- Required tokens/sec at peak: 9k concurrent requests * (200 tokens / avg response time window). For SLO compute we use throughput-limited window: if p95 target is 0.9s per 200 tokens, then each session consumes ~222 tokens/sec demand (200 tokens / 0.9s) -> per-request token rate not right; better approach:}

NOTE (we walked through two approaches; recorded the one we landed on):
Approach A: Request-per-second (RPS) based
- Estimate peak RPS for short-turn: assume 9k concurrent users, average think time between messages 45s => RPS = 9000/45 = 200 RPS peak
- Each short-turn request asks for 200 tokens (generation). If model stream can produce 200 tokens in 0.9s, then tokens/sec demand = RPS * tokens = 200 * 200 = 40,000 tokens/sec peak
- For 13B on A100-40GB (we used 300 tokens/sec per GPU nominal) => GPUs needed = 40,000 / 300 ≈ 133 GPUs. With 65% utilization target, provision = 133 / 0.65 ≈ 205 GPUs.
- For 70B on H100 equiv (nominal 900 tokens/sec) => GPUs needed = 40,000 / 900 ≈ 45 GPUs. With utilization headroom => 45 / 0.65 ≈ 70 GPUs.

Approach B: Latency-first headroom (preferred for production SLOs)
- Start from desired p95 latency and maximum in-flight tokens/GPU at target batch sizes. Example: if a single GPU can concurrently sustain 4 in-flight requests with average 200 tokens at p95 latency, then per-GPU concurrent sessions = 4 -> need = 9000/4 = 2250 GPUs (obviously unrealistic). This approach is conservative and we use it only for very strict latency products.

Decision from workshop: Use Approach A for initial Dedicated sizing with conservative utilization buffer. Approach B flagged as too conservative except for sub-100ms SLOs.

Autoscaling policy template (proposal-ready):
- Metrics used to scale up/down:
  1) queued_request_count / avg_request_size_tokens (primary) -> scale up when > X tokens pending (maps to token processing backlog).
  2) GPU utilization (secondary) -> scale up when sustained > 75% for 90s across cluster.
  3) tail_latency p95 > target_latency (preference: triggered scale up + canary route to lower-quality model).
- Scale up behavior:
  - Policy: add N GPUs (min 2, max 10 per scale event) when queued_tokens > 2x capacity of current cluster. Immediate cold-starts: prefer warm pool or reserved burst capacity to avoid cold-container penalties.
  - Warm pool: keep 5% of min_capacity as warm replicas (hot kernels preloaded) and 10% extra as fast-start cached images for rapid additions (startup < 30s target).
- Scale down behavior:
  - Cooldown: require sustained low demand (queued_tokens < 25% capacity and gpu_util < 40%) for 10 minutes before removing GPUs.
  - Prefer removing least recently used nodes, gracefully drain KV cache to avoid token re-gen costs.
- Pre-warming and burst lanes:
  - Reserve a small burst capacity (1.2x min capacity) that can be spun up using preloaded images in < 30s for traffic spikes. For customers with very spiky QPS, allocate dedicated burst node pool (separate pool billing).

Quantization and model variant routing guidance:
- Default: 13B quantized q4_0 for low-cost routes (fallbacks and most user queries that can accept slightly lower quality).
- Quality-critical: 70B fp16 or q4f16 on H100 with response-ranking + safety evals.
- Routing rule sample (for Proposal):
  - If route == "search/summarize" and doc_size < 30KB -> 13B (fast); if human-flag or QA-confidence < 0.7 -> route to 70B for re-run and final answer.
  - If route == "checkout-or-trade-decision" -> always 70B.

GPU cost estimate (baseline for proposal):
- For proposal we prefer to show two columns: Infra-equivalent unit price (market) and Redwood customer-facing committed price (monthly commit discount example). These are illustrative numbers for the POC; final numbers to be pulled from finance.
  - H100-80GB equivalent (reserved pricing): market infra cost ≈ $6.50/hr GPU (on-demand equiv), suggested committed price to customer (incl platform overhead) ≈ $9.00/hr/GPU. Assumptions: reserved infra at 50% discount vs on-demand, plus platform + SRE overheads.
  - A100-40GB equivalent: market infra cost ≈ $2.80/hr, suggested committed price ≈ $4.00/hr/GPU.
- Using the Approach A sizing numbers:
  - 13B path: 205 A100-equivalent GPUs * $4.00/hr = $820/hr => ~ $19,680/day (24h) => ~$590k/month (30d). Flag: this is the top-line Dedicated compute only; excludes storage, network egress, monitoring retention, and onboarding/engineering fees.
  - 70B path: 70 H100-equivalent GPUs * $9.00/hr = $630/hr => ~$15,120/day => ~$454k/month.
- Notes on cost levers we can propose to customer to reduce burn:
  1) aggressive quantization (q5/q6 research) or product engineering to reduce average generation length (prompt engineering, caching summaries). Potential 30–60% token savings.
  2) intelligent routing + caching for repeat queries (hot-prefix caching) could reduce effective RPS by 20–40% depending on domain.
  3) spot/interruptible for non-critical batch jobs (re-rankers, offline summaries) up to 70% lower infra cost; but not for primary low-latency path.

POC scope recommendation (3-week POC):
- Week 0: Integration + telemetry (ingest sample traffic, wire up observability). Baseline: run 2x A100 equiv and 1x H100 equiv as canary/baseline.
- Week 1: Latency profiling, quantization sweep, and batch tuning. Goal: firm up tokens/sec and p95 numbers for 13B and 70B under customer prompt distribution.
- Week 2: Autoscale policy trial with synthetic spikes and warm-pool tests. Validate scale up in < 45s with warm pool and < 90s cold start.
- Deliverable: POC report with measured tokens/sec/GPU, suggested committed capacity, expected monthly cost, and a proposed autoscale config to deploy in Dedicated.

Open questions / risks flagged:
- Lab throughput numbers are high-variance across sequence length and attention patterns. Need customer sample corpus to run more realistic perf tests.
- KV cache effectiveness unknown: if customers do long multi-turn chat with large context windows, effective tokens/sec per GPU will drop significantly.
- Dedicated pricing model: final customer price needs finance approval; we used placeholder multipliers.

Action items (owners):
- Miguel: run perf sweep with customer sample prompts for 13B + 70B on infra staging (due 2026-03-17).
- Aisha: draft one-page cost summary with tiered committed discounts and add-on pricing for warm pools and burst lanes (due 2026-03-20).
- Claire: prototype autoscale config as YAML + Terraform snippets for dedicated cluster: include warm pool toggles and drain behavior (due 2026-03-22).
- Daniel: create a short customer slide deck (3 slides) summarizing tradeoffs and recommended POC scope (due 2026-03-19).

Notes to include in customer-facing proposal (quick bullets):
- We recommend starting POC with a mixed-variant approach: 13B quantized for most routes and a small H100-backed 70B pool for quality-critical traffic; this lowers baseline cost while ensuring quality for the important flows.
- Commit to measurable evaluation criteria: latency SLOs, cost per 1k sessions, and answer quality thresholds via 50 sample prompts (A/B between variants).
- Include an operational runbook: warm pool size, incident playbook for cascade failures, and fallback to lower-quality variant.

Appendix (raw math snippets used during workshop):
- Peak RPS estimate = concurrent_users / avg_think_time.
- Token demand = RPS * avg_tokens_per_request.
- GPUs_required = ceil(Token_demand / tokens_per_sec_per_gpu) / utilization_target.
- Example live calc (short-turn): RPS=200, tokens/request=200 -> tokens/sec=40k; 13B gpu nominal 300 tps -> 40k/300 = 133 -> provision 205 @65% target.

End of notes.


Quick personal notes: keep the POC conservative on initial min_capacity (we should over-provision a bit to avoid showing the customer a flaky demo). The numbers can be massively reduced if the customer accepts longer tail latencies or pushes more work into async pipelines.
